how-much-can-i-raise-my-saas-price.html.text:
← Subscription price impact calculator

How much can I raise my SaaS price?

A price increase does not have to cause zero churn to be worth doing — it only has to cause less churn than the break-even rate. Raising price without knowing that number means guessing whether the customers you'll lose are a rounding error or the whole gain, wiped out.

Open the free SaaS price impact calculator

What a flat percentage increase cannot see

Break-even churn, not zero churn. The revenue break-even point is the subscriber count where current price × current subscribers equals proposed price × subscribers left. A 25% increase can lose a fifth of subscribers and still bill the same as before the change.

Fixed costs do not move with churn. Contribution (revenue minus your fixed monthly costs) reacts to the same churn scenarios differently than revenue alone, because the fixed-cost line stays constant while revenue shifts under it.

Five scenarios, not one guess. The calculator prices 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% churn side by side, so you can see exactly where contribution stops improving and starts falling.

A number you can defend

  1. Enter active subscribers, current monthly price, proposed monthly price, and monthly fixed costs.
  2. Read the maximum churn rate: the subscriber loss that still leaves revenue at or above today's level.
  3. Check the subscribers-at-break-even figure — the exact headcount, not just a percentage.
  4. Compare contribution, not just revenue, across all five churn scenarios before deciding.

Worked example

100 subscribers pay $20 a month ($2,000 current revenue) against $500 in monthly fixed costs. Raising the price to $25 puts revenue break-even at 80 subscribers — a maximum churn rate of 20% before revenue falls below $2,000. At exactly 20% churn, 80 subscribers remain, revenue is $2,000, and contribution is $1,500 — unchanged from before the increase because fixed costs stayed at $500. At a more likely 10% churn, 90 subscribers remain, revenue rises to $2,250, and contribution rises to $1,750 — $250 better than before the price ever moved.

Common questions

How much can I raise my SaaS price before losing revenue to churn?

The break-even churn rate is 1 minus the ratio of your old price to your new price. Raising price from $20 to $25 is a 25% increase, and the ratio 20/25 = 0.8 means recurring revenue stays at or above today's level up to 20% subscriber churn. Above that, even though each remaining subscriber pays more, revenue falls below where it started.

What if the price increase itself causes exactly that much churn?

At exactly the break-even churn rate, revenue lands back where it started — 100 subscribers at $20 and 80 subscribers at $25 both bill $2,000 a month. Contribution (revenue minus fixed costs) also lands unchanged, because fixed costs do not move with subscriber count. Any churn below that rate leaves both revenue and contribution higher than before the increase.

Does this account for fixed costs, not just revenue?

Yes. The calculator subtracts your entered monthly fixed costs from projected revenue at each of five churn scenarios — 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%, and 20% — so you can see contribution, not just top-line revenue, at each churn level before deciding.

Common questions

How much churn can a price increase actually absorb?

On the default example — 100 subscribers going from $20 to $25 a month — revenue reaches the same $2,000 you make today at just 80 subscribers, so you can lose up to 20 of the current 100 (20% churn) before the increase has cost you anything. That 20% is not a prediction of how many people will actually leave; it is the ceiling this specific increase can absorb before it stops paying off. “Subscribers at revenue break-even” and the churn-scenario table show the same number two ways.

Why does a price decrease show 0% maximum churn?

Because break-even is measured in revenue, and cutting the price raises the subscriber count needed to match today's revenue above the count you already have. Drop $20 to $15 on the same 100 subscribers and break-even needs about 133 — more than you have — so the calculator reports zero headroom: any churn at all, even churn that had nothing to do with the price cut, drops you below where you started. This tool does not model new customers a lower price might attract; it only tracks retention of the base you already have.

Is “subscribers at revenue break-even” the same as break-even on profit?

No. That figure is revenue against revenue — it ignores costs entirely. The profit view is the contribution column in the churn-scenario table, which nets your monthly fixed costs out of revenue at each churn level. A price change can clear the revenue break-even and still fail to clear the contribution break-even if your fixed costs are large relative to the price change.

What does “contribution” leave out?

Only the monthly fixed costs you type in. It does not subtract payment-processing fees, support cost per seat, hosting that scales with usage, or anything else that moves with subscriber count rather than staying flat month to month. If a meaningful share of your costs are variable, contribution overstates the profit impact of both the increase and the churn.

Why does the churn-scenario table stop at 20%?

Those five columns (0, 5, 10, 15, 20%) are a representative spread for sanity-checking a scenario, not a forecast bounded at 20%. Churn above that is entirely possible and the table simply does not print it; use your own historical churn rate, not the table's range, to judge whether a given increase is likely to land above or below its break-even point.

vs-baremetrics.html.text:
← Subscription price impact calculator

This calculator vs. Baremetrics

Baremetrics is a subscription-analytics platform. You connect a live billing source — natively Stripe, Braintree, Recurly, or Chargebee, with CSV import or its API for others — and it reports MRR, churn, LTV, and related metrics computed from the subscribers you already have, on an ongoing dashboard. It is a paid product: sign-up starts a free trial, and continued use is a paid subscription, described on baremetrics.com.

That makes it the right choice for one job: watching the metrics your real, connected subscription business is already producing, over time. This page does not do that job. It has no billing connection, keeps no dashboard, and reports on nothing that already happened.

QuestionWhere to answer it
What is my actual MRR, churn rate, and LTV right now, computed from my real Stripe (or other) subscription data? Baremetrics — that is a live reporting job built on data this calculator never sees.
If I raise (or lower) the price from $X to $Y, how much subscriber churn can revenue absorb before it falls? This calculator — type in the two prices, the subscriber count, and fixed costs, get the break-even churn rate instantly, no signup, nothing connected.
I have not made the change yet and do not want to connect a billing account to test the idea — can I still see the number? This calculator — it runs entirely on numbers you type, before or without ever connecting Stripe or any other processor.
Does the price change still clear break-even once my fixed monthly costs are netted out, not just top-line revenue? This calculator's contribution column — five churn scenarios (0, 5, 10, 15, 20%) with fixed costs subtracted at each one.
What actually happened to revenue and churn in the months after I made a price change? Baremetrics, or your own billing reports — this calculator only projects forward from numbers you type in for a scenario; it stores nothing and reconciles nothing against what actually happened.

Many SaaS operators use a tool like this one to size up a price change before touching pricing, and a connected platform like Baremetrics to watch what a real subscriber base does afterward — the two are not substitutes for each other. This calculator's own churn scenarios are a planning aid, not a prediction: your own historical churn rate, wherever you track it (Baremetrics or otherwise), is a better input than the table's five representative columns.

It needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or Baremetrics?

They answer different questions at different points in the decision. Baremetrics is a subscription-analytics platform: you connect a live billing source such as Stripe, Braintree, Recurly, or Chargebee (or import a CSV), and it reports MRR, churn, and other metrics computed from the subscribers you actually have. It is a paid, ongoing product with a free trial to start, described on Baremetrics's own site. This page has no data connection and reports on nothing you already have. It takes a hypothetical subscriber count, current price, proposed price, and fixed cost you type in, and shows the maximum churn a specific price change can absorb before revenue falls, instantly, for free, with no signup and nothing connected. A SaaS operator deciding whether a price increase is worth trying is in the right place here; one who wants an ongoing dashboard of the metrics their real, connected subscription base is already producing wants Baremetrics.

Is this page affiliated with Baremetrics?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by Baremetrics. Baremetrics is named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not, based on Baremetrics's own public site and help documentation.
